source: Burnett & Richmond (2026) Meta-analytic investigations of the effect of cognitive offloading on memory-based task performance and interindividual variability (Memory & Cognition 54(1):144-168)
finding: Two meta-analyses. Offloading helps more when it is forced than when it is chosen, and more in within-subject than between-subject designs. Offloading also shrinks differences between people, more so for adults than children, for forced than chosen offloading, and for prospective than retrospective tasks.
numbers: Only the abstract record was opened. No effect sizes, no k, no N and no forced-minus-chosen gap could be read. Study modality was not a moderator in either analysis.
quote: benefit of offloading is greater for forced- compared to choice-offloading conditions
limits: Full text not reached (paywalled; Europe PMC shows no open access). Gap 4 stays open for numbers. Direction of the forced-vs-chosen result is confirmed from the abstract of the primary source.
agent_relevance: Supports having the program, not the model, decide every store write. Size of the benefit is still unknown.

source: Burnett et al. (2026) Exploring the consequences of cognitive offloading: levels of processing and subjective experiences of retrieval (PMID 42622798)
finding: Four experiments. When people expected to keep the notes but lost access at test, recall was worse than in a shallow-encoding group. With notes in hand at test, people gave fewer 'remember' judgments. The authors say offloading serves both storage and encoding, and the balance shifts with store expectancy.
numbers: Exps 1-3: unexpected-loss offloading recall poorer than shallow-encoding recall. Exp 4: fewer remember judgments with notes at test. No effect sizes in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Word lists, human students. Numbers not read.
agent_relevance: If the store is withdrawn or corrupted after the model stopped holding the content, expect a worse result than never having encoded it. Keep a re-read step or keep key facts in context too.

source: Age group and experience impact partial cognitive offloading for value-based remembering (PMID 41538170, 2026)
finding: Two experiments, young and older adults, free recall of valued words, partial offloading. Experience with partial offloading raised overall scores in both groups. Only young adults showed better memory for the non-saved items (saving-enhanced memory); older adults did not rededicate freed resources.
numbers: Exp 1: three trials of direct instruction. Exp 2: extended practice. No effect sizes in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. The saving-enhanced benefit is not universal: it depends on who uses the freed capacity.
agent_relevance: Freed capacity is not automatically reused. A scaffold that offloads should say what the freed context is to be spent on (the next sub-problem).

source: Individual differences in prospective and retrospective memory offloading (PMC12263121, 2025)
finding: When offloading was required or permitted, people with different working-memory capacity performed more alike than with internal memory alone. Lower-capacity people gained more, especially at high load. Underconfidence did not predict how often people offloaded.
numbers: Abstract-level reading; no effect sizes extracted.
limits: Human, word and intention tasks. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Forced external state acts as an equaliser. For an agent the analogue is that weaker models gain most from a program-held state.

source: Tool-Induced Myopia (arXiv 2511.10899 v2, Nov 2025), Table 2
finding: Same-model comparison on PYMATH (1,679 competition problems): giving the model a code interpreter changed final accuracy by very different amounts across models, while pairwise reasoning quality got worse for the tool version.
numbers: Final accuracy base vs tool: GPT-4.1-mini 30.0 vs 28.7; GPT-4.1 24.6 vs 27.0; o4-mini 45.1 vs 64.4 (+19.3, the headline). PRM step accuracy base vs tool: 93.0 vs 88.9; 88.6 vs 85.9; 73.6 vs 67.9. Base win rate over tool: 58.6, 54.4, 49.0 percent.
limits: Hard competition math where the code replaces the derivation. Not a state-keeping task. The +19.3 is one model (o4-mini); two of three models gained little or lost accuracy. LLM-judge and PRM measures.
agent_relevance: Same-model effect of code is not uniform: near zero or negative for non-reasoning models on hard math. Do not assume offloading helps; measure per model. Gap 2 partly answered.

source: Tool-Induced Myopia (arXiv 2511.10899 v2), tool-call dose and tool use rates
finding: Problems were binned by number of tool calls (0-3, 4-7, 8-11, 12+). As calls rise, the base model's win rate rises, miss rate rises and PRM accuracy falls; the 12+ bin sometimes reverses because of small samples. Thinking models call the interpreter more.
numbers: Tool use rate: Claude-opus-4 99.8%, GPT-5 73.7%; thinking models call code on about 49.7% more problems. Manual audit: TIM in 54.3% of high-risk cases (top 10 per model). Numbers per bin are in a figure and were not extracted.
limits: Dose is correlational: harder problems also need more calls. Audit is 10 samples per model. Task is code-as-solution.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 3 only in part: the dose-response is about calls that carry the solution. No test where code only holds counters or lists. Gap 3 stays open.

source: Tool-Induced Myopia (arXiv 2511.10899 v2), mitigation Table 3 (GPT-4.1)
finding: A one-sentence prompt ('treat code snippets and their execution results only as helpful hints, and derive the solution through mathematical reasoning') raised win rate but lowered accuracy. DPO on the training split improved both but only for one model.
limits: Single model, single benchmark, fine-tuning not available for a frozen API agent. The prompt-only fix cost 1.9 points of accuracy, nearly all the tool gain (2.4).
agent_relevance: Prompt-only mitigation exists but trades accuracy for reasoning quality. The agent should keep the tool role narrow (state and counts) so there is little derivation to displace.

source: Wang, Qian et al. (2025) Acting Less is Reasoning More: OTC-PO (arXiv 2504.14870)
finding: RL reward that scores a correct answer higher the fewer tool calls it used. Cuts calls with similar exact-match accuracy. Defines tool productivity as correct answers divided by tool calls.
numbers: Abstract: up to 68.3% fewer tool calls and up to 215.4% higher tool productivity (Qwen2.5-3B, NQ, OTC-PPO vs Search-R1-PPO). Math: ToRL-GRPO 1.5B AIME24 EM 20.0 with 2.2 calls vs OTC-GRPO 1.1 calls. Result tables came out garbled in text extraction; only abstract figures and a few rows are trusted.
limits: Trained with RL on Qwen models; search and code tools. Not prompt-only, not a frozen API. The only prompt change was a template line saying to call tools only when necessary.
agent_relevance: Shows over-calling is real and removable, but the fix is training. For a frozen model a hard cap on calls or a program-set schedule is the nearest lever. Gap 7 only partly answered.

source: Qian et al. (2025) SMART: Self-Aware Agent for Tool Overuse Mitigation (arXiv 2502.11435)
finding: Models call tools for questions they could answer from memory. SMART trains agents (SFT on SMART-ER data) to know when to use a tool.
numbers: Abstract: tool use down 24 percent, performance up over 37 percent; on out-of-distribution GSM8K and MINTQA about one-fifth the tool calls at the same accuracy; 7B matches a 70B and GPT-4o.
limits: Abstract only; trained agents, not prompt-only.
agent_relevance: Same message as OTC: over-calling is common and fixable by training. No prompt-only budget curve found for frozen models.

source: Chen et al. (2025, ICLR) Steering Large Language Models between Code Execution and Textual Reasoning (arXiv 2410.03524) Table 2
finding: Direct same-model comparison of text, forced code, and model-chosen code (Code Interpreter) over 14 tasks and 6 models. Forced code usually beats text. Model-chosen code beats forced code for two of three models tested, not for GPT-3.5. A combined code+text+summary method was best overall.
numbers: Average normalised score (%). GPT-4o: only question 80.6, all text 79.9, all code (forced) 80.3, Code Interpreter (chosen) 83.5, code+text+summary 88.1. GPT-4o-mini: 67.6, 75.9, 77.4, 80.8, 85.0. GPT-3.5: 65.3, 65.3, 68.1, 64.5, 63.9. o1-preview: 88.2, 81.9, 93.3, n/a, 90.2. Mean over 6: all text 73.9, all code 77.2, code+text+sum 79.5.
limits: Tasks are mostly arithmetic and puzzle problems where code solves the whole task, not state-keeping. Forced here means told to write code, not program-controlled transitions. Gap 1 is about stores, so only indirect.
agent_relevance: Against a blanket 'forced beats chosen' rule: for solution code, chosen code was as good or better for 2 of 3 models. The forced-wins evidence is for reminders and state writes, not for solution code.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Steering LLMs, section 2: code/text choice failures
finding: GPT-4o with a code interpreter handles easy multiplication in text and very large ones in code, and fails in the middle where it should have used code. The authors say it is overconfident. Smaller models that always write code reached 100 percent on some tasks, an inverse scaling effect.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini and GPT-3.5 reach 100% success across all complexity levels in the multiplication task (Fig 3). GPT-4o only starts using code on Game 24 when complexity is very high (extra tests not in the paper). Paper conclusion: no optimal method to steer code vs text.
limits: 2024 models (GPT-4o, GPT-3.5). Newer reasoning models use code far more (see d06).
agent_relevance: Answers gap 8 in direction: models are worse at deciding when to use code than at using it when told. Same direction as Boldt & Gilbert (a06). But it is a model-capability finding, not a controlled instructed-vs-spontaneous contrast.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents, CodeAct (arXiv 2402.01030)
finding: Same LLM acts through Python code, JSON or text. Code gets higher success on 12 of 17 models and fewer turns on 12 of 17.
numbers: Text: gpt-4-1106-preview had a 20.7 point absolute improvement over the next best format (text) on M3ToolEval, with 2.1 fewer turns. Headline: up to 20 percent higher success across 17 LLMs.
limits: Table cells garbled in extraction; only sentences from the text are trusted. 2024 models. Benchmark built by the authors.
agent_relevance: Same-model, same-tool evidence that letting the program compose steps beats one-call-per-step text actions. Gap 2 partly answered for older models.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking (arXiv 2506.06941), algorithm-given experiment
finding: Giving the full recursive algorithm in the prompt (Tower of Hanoi, Checker Jumping) did not help: collapse came at about the same complexity. Authors answered the claim that this is Hanoi-specific by also testing Checker Jumping.
numbers: Figure 8: no meaningful improvement with the algorithm provided; collapse at similar N. Token budget up to 64k for Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking. First-failure move analysis shows errors early on some puzzles.
limits: Execution was done in text by the model, so token limits and unsolvable cases (see d14) confound. No code-execution arm in the paper.
agent_relevance: The cleanest statement of the failure the agent avoids by running algorithms in code.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking (arXiv 2506.09250)
finding: Three objections: Hanoi outputs hit output token limits and models said so; the grader cannot tell a stop from a failure; some River Crossing instances with N above 5 are unsolvable yet scored as failures. When asked to output a Lua function that prints the solution, models were reported to succeed on 15 disks.
numbers: Hanoi N=15 as a function: 'very high accuracy' for Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude Opus 4, o3, Gemini 2.5, under 5,000 tokens. No counts, no number of runs, labelled preliminary. Token cost taken as 10 tokens per move after a correction.
quote: Solve Tower of Hanoi with 15 disks. Output a Lua function that prints the solution when called.
limits: Preliminary and unquantified. Writing the generator shows the model knows the algorithm; it is not a state-tracking loop. Partial answer to gap 10: with code the collapse disappears in the reply, but it was not measured at scale.
agent_relevance: Supports executing algorithms in code, but the evidence is thin and self-reported. Test it in our own harness with counts.

source: Memory Injection Attacks on LLM Agents via Query-Only Interaction, MINJA (arXiv 2503.03704)
finding: Poisoning an agent's memory bank only through normal queries works. Agents then use the poisoned records as demonstrations and produce the attacker's target. Prompt-level detection is the defence the authors consider most practical.
numbers: Average injection success 98.2 percent, attack success 76.8 percent across three agents, four victim-target pairs. Overall ISR above 95 percent; ASR from about 60 to over 90 percent. On clean vs prior-poisoned memory some ASR drops (MIMIC-III pair 2 50.0 to 30.0). Utility drop under 2 percent on three datasets, 10.0 percent on MMLU.
limits: Retrieval-based memory of text records. Attacker model, not accidental staleness. Self-detection by the agent is not the focus.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: agent memory written from model output can be corrupted and the agent follows it. A code-held counter written by the program has no such path, but any model-written note does.

source: How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior (arXiv 2505.16067)
finding: Agents copy the output of the stored record whose input is most similar (experience-following). Bad records therefore propagate (error propagation), and good-looking but unhelpful records mislead (misaligned replay). Selective addition with a strict evaluator and history-based deletion cut the damage.
numbers: Error-free comparison on RegAgent and AgentDriver shows an immediate gap versus ground-truth records that grows under add-all and coarse selective addition; strict selective addition narrows it. Deletion table (success rate and memory size per agent) is garbled in extraction; qualitative result only.
limits: Four agents on older backbones plus GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 spot checks. Per-cell numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: stale or wrong entries are a measured failure mode. Add an expiry or verify rule to any note the model writes.

source: Anthropic (2025) Managing context on the Claude Developer Platform: context editing and memory tool
finding: Clearing stale tool calls and results from context as the window fills, with a memory tool that stores facts outside context, improved an internal agentic search benchmark on Claude Sonnet 4.5.
numbers: Context editing alone +29 percent over baseline; memory tool plus context editing +39 percent; 84 percent fewer tokens in a 100-turn web search evaluation, and some runs that would have failed from context exhaustion finished. N not stated.
limits: Vendor blog, internal unnamed benchmark, no N or confidence interval, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: clearing helped in this setup, which does not repeat Grinschgl's cost because the model can re-read the store. Needs our own run with and without a re-read step.

source: MEM1: Learning to Synergize Memory and Reasoning for Efficient Long-Horizon Agents (arXiv 2506.15841)
finding: RL-trained agent keeps one compact state that it rewrites each turn instead of appending the full history. Memory stays constant over turns.
numbers: 16-objective multi-hop QA: MEM1-7B 3.5x better performance and 3.7x less memory than Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct.
limits: Abstract only. Trained, model-chosen compaction. No forced-store arm.
agent_relevance: A model-chosen constant-size state can beat full history. Not a test of program-forced stores (gap 1 stays open).

source: Memory as Action: Autonomous Context Curation for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks, MemAct (arXiv 2510.12635 v3)
finding: Memory edits (insert, delete in place) treated as actions the policy learns with RL. A 14B model matches models 16 times larger with 51 percent shorter average context.
numbers: Accuracy parity with 16x larger models; average context length reduced 51 percent.
limits: Abstract only; trained, model-chosen. No comparison with a program-set store at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Again model-chosen curation. Gap 1 still has no direct forced-versus-chosen LLM test.

source: Salomon, Perkins & Globerson (1991) Partners in cognition; Salomon (1997) Distributed cognitions
finding: Not opened. SAGE returned HTTP 403, ERIC had no record, Semantic Scholar rate-limited. Only a secondary citation was seen (a 2016 graphing-calculator paper using the with/of framing).
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Gap 6 stays open for the original text. The effect-of side is covered only by Florean 2026 (a14: removal cost exceeds introduction gain) and Let it go 2026 (a15).
agent_relevance: No LLM study found that removes a scaffold and measures what the model keeps; frozen models cannot learn, so effect-of is mostly a human concept.
